english: clueless / out of your depth (youth slang)
whenToUse: Pronounced like the English word and used as an adjective: "Du bist lost" means you have no idea what is going on. Teasing among friends and classmates, fine in a group chat, odd with your boss.
example: Ohne Navi bin ich total lost.

whenToUse: Teens and twenty-somethings say "Das ist so cringe" about awkward behaviour or bad jokes. It's harmless, but telling someone their own act is cringe can sting, so aim it at things, not at people.
example: Dieses Video ist so cringe.

english: crazy / unbelievable (in a good or shocked way)
whenToUse: Used as a reaction to a surprising story: "Wild!" or "Das ist wild!". Friendly and neutral, works with anyone under about 50.
example: Er ist einfach aus dem Fenster gesprungen? Das ist wild!

whenToUse: A warm compliment among younger people for someone who did you a favour: "Danke, du Ehrenmann!". Use Ehrenfrau for women. Slightly jokey, so keep it for friends.
example: Du hast mir geholfen? Du bist ein Ehrenmann!

english: suspicious / dodgy (from the game Among Us)
whenToUse: Gamer-born slang, pronounced "sass". Said about someone or something that seems off: "Das ist sus." Only works with people who play or watch games, and it will date quickly.
example: Der Typ ist komisch. Voll sus.

whenToUse: Everyday and relaxed: "Wir chillen heute" means nothing special is planned. It's a regular verb (ich chille, du chillst), fine with friends and coworkers, but not in a formal email.
example: Lass uns am Sonntag einfach chillen.

whenToUse: Encouraging a friend to enjoy something: "Gönn dir ein Eis!". "Gönnen" can also be said about someone who spends a lot: "Er gönnt sich was." Friendly and positive, used mostly by younger speakers.
example: Du hast Geburtstag? Gönn dir ein Stück Kuchen!

whenToUse: Literally "it's running for you". It can be a sincere compliment or sarcasm, depending on tone. If the person has just spilled their coffee, it's definitely sarcasm. Among friends only.
example: Neue Wohnung, neuer Job? Läuft bei dir!

whenToUse: Youth slang from the city: "Kommst du?" "Safe!" means yes without any doubt. Casual and friendly, but it can sound odd outside a younger crowd.
example: Wir sehen uns später? Safe!

whenToUse: A friendly way for young men (and some women) to address friends, mostly in cities: "Alles gut, Bruder?". With strangers it can sound pushy or like you are trying to pick a fight, so wait until you know the tone.
example: Danke, Bruder, du hast mir echt geholfen.

whenToUse: Typical Berlin speech: "Ick liebe dit" instead of "Ich liebe das". Locals use it all the time, and it's fine to enjoy it as a visitor, but don't overdo it or it sounds like mockery.
example: Ick weeß ooch nich.

whenToUse: Short for "nicht wahr", tacked on the end of a sentence in Berlin: "Is' schön hier, wa?". Friendly and chatty. Elsewhere people say "oder?" or "ne?".
example: Das schaffen wir, wa?

whenToUse: What Berliners call a plain bread roll. Order "zwei Schrippen" at a Berlin bakery and nobody blinks. In Bavaria it's a Semmel, and in the Rhineland a Weckchen, so the word marks you as a local.
example: Zwei Schrippen mit Butter, bitte.

whenToUse: A standard polite greeting in the south, used with shopkeepers, neighbours and strangers of any age. It isn't really religious in practice. In northern Germany nobody says it, so you'd sound like a tourist.
example: Grüß Gott, einen Kaffee bitte.

whenToUse: Viennese and Austrian slang: it can show surprise ("Oida!"), anger or affection. Between friends it's fine. Calling a stranger or an older person "Oida" can sound rude, so listen first and copy the tone.
example: Oida, das glaub ich nicht!

english: it's fine / no worries (Bavarian for "passt schon")
whenToUse: A relaxed Bavarian way to say "that's OK", "keep the change" or "no problem". It's friendly and common in the south, and understood everywhere, but it sounds odd from someone in Hamburg.
example: Danke fürs Warten! Passt scho.

whenToUse: A warm, informal goodbye in the south. Use "Pfiat Ihnen" to be polite. Servus also works for goodbye there, but Pfiat di sounds more local.
example: Bis morgen, pfiat di!

whenToUse: The standard greeting in German-speaking Switzerland, used with shopkeepers, hotel staff and strangers. Safe and respectful. Swiss friends may say "Hoi" instead.
example: Grüezi, ich hätte gern ein Ticket.

english: what are you doing? (short for "was machst du?")
whenToUse: Texting shorthand between friends: "wmd?" Usually the opening of a casual chat, similar to "wyd" in English. Don't use it in work messages or with older relatives who might not know it.
example: Hey, wmd heute Abend?

whenToUse: Even shorter than "kA": "kein Plan" means you really don't know, written as kp. Texts and chats only, and fine with friends, but too casual for a work email.
example: Wann fängt der Film an? kp.

whenToUse: A warm sign-off in texts and informal emails, a little more affectionate than "lg". Fine for friends, family and friendly colleagues. In a formal email, write out "Mit freundlichen Grüßen".
example: Bis bald! vlg Anna

english: love you lots ("hab dich ganz doll lieb")
whenToUse: A sweet, affectionate sign-off for partners, close friends and family, often followed by a heart. Slightly childlike, which is part of the charm. Don't send it to a colleague.
example: Gute Nacht, hdgdl!

whenToUse: A wordplay shorthand from chat: "Nacht" rhymes with "acht", so "gn8" works. Friends and family only, and only at bedtime.
example: Ich geh schlafen. gn8!

whenToUse: A mild, old-fashioned exclamation of surprise, often with a grin. Safe in nearly any setting, though a bit northern-sounding. It's often said by people over 40.
example: Alter Schwede, ist das teuer!

whenToUse: Said when something goes wrong: "Na toll, der Zug ist weg." It's sarcasm with a sigh. Safe to use anywhere, as long as it's not directed at a person's face.
example: Na toll, jetzt regnet es auch noch.

whenToUse: Common in Bavaria and Austria, used for someone who made a silly mistake: "Du Depp!". Among friends it's affectionate teasing. Said to a stranger, it's a real insult.
example: Ich bin so ein Depp, ich habe den Schlüssel vergessen.

whenToUse: A stronger version of "Quatsch": "Das ist doch Schwachsinn!". It's a harsh way to dismiss an idea, so don't say it about your boss's plan or a stranger's opinion. Fine about a news story or a rumour.
example: Das ist doch alles Schwachsinn.

english: you must be mad / you're nuts
whenToUse: Said when someone suggests something crazy. It's rude but not vulgar, and with friends it can be joking. Never use it in a calm argument, because it escalates quickly.
example: Um drei Uhr nachts? Du hast doch einen Knall!

whenToUse: Vulgar emphasis on "egal": "Das ist mir scheißegal." Heard constantly among friends and in anger, but it's rude in front of strangers, elders or at work. If you want a polite version, say "Das ist mir egal".
example: Mir ist scheißegal, was die anderen denken.

english: are you kidding me? / are you taking the mickey?
whenToUse: Vulgar and confrontational: you think someone is making a fool of you. Between friends it's a shocked reaction to a prank. Said to a stranger or a boss it's an insult.
example: Das Ticket kostet fünfzig Euro? Willst du mich verarschen?

english: shut your face / shut up (very rude)
whenToUse: Much ruder than "Halt die Klappe". It's a real insult, used in fights or between very close friends who joke around. As a learner, you can recognise it, but never use it.
example: Halt die Fresse, ich will das nicht hören!
